title: HTTP: requests, responses and status codes
intro: HTTP is the language browsers and servers use to communicate on the web. In this lesson, you will learn what an HTTP request and response contain, what the common methods and status codes mean, and how to inspect real requests in your browser.
body:
## What is HTTP?

**HTTP** stands for Hypertext Transfer Protocol. It is a set of rules that describes how a client, such as your browser, communicates with a server.

You can think of HTTP as a conversation:

~~~text
Browser: Please give me the products.
Server: Here they are.
~~~

In reality, the browser sends a structured **request**, and the server sends a structured **response**.

HTTP is not only used to load web pages. Modern applications use it constantly to exchange data. A React application might use HTTP to load products, create an account, update a profile, or delete a saved item.

In this course, React will communicate with our Spring Boot backend using HTTP.

## An HTTP request

An HTTP request tells a server what the client wants to do.

~~~diagram
{"type": "layers", "title": "Anatomy of a request", "layers": [{"label": "Request line", "sub": "method + path + version", "items": ["GET /api/tasks?done=false HTTP/1.1"], "highlight": true}, {"label": "Headers", "sub": "metadata as key: value", "items": ["Host: shop.example.com", "Accept: application/json", "Authorization: Bearer …"]}, {"label": "Empty line", "sub": "ends the headers"}, {"label": "Body (optional)", "sub": "POST / PUT / PATCH data", "items": ["{ \"title\": \"Buy milk\" }"]}]}
~~~

A request can contain four important parts:

- **Method** — what kind of operation you want to perform.
- **URL** — which resource you want to access.
- **Headers** — additional information about the request.
- **Body** — optional data sent to the server.

For example, a browser could send a request like this:

~~~http
POST /api/products HTTP/1.1
Host: shop.example.com
Content-Type: application/json
Accept: application/json
Authorization: Bearer example-token

{
  "name": "Running shoes",
  "price": 89.99
}
~~~

The first line says that this is a `POST` request for `/api/products`.

The `Host` header identifies the host being contacted. `Content-Type` tells the server what format the request body uses. `Accept` tells the server which response format the client would prefer.

The body contains the actual product data.

Not every request has a body. A typical `GET` request, for example, usually does not need one.

## HTTP methods

The **HTTP method** describes the intended operation.

### GET — read data

`GET` is normally used when you want to retrieve data.

For example:

~~~http
GET /api/products
~~~

A browser could use this request to retrieve a list of products.

Another example might be:

~~~http
GET /api/products/42
~~~

This could request product number 42.

A GET request should generally not be used to change data on the server.

### POST — create or submit

`POST` is commonly used to create a new resource or submit data for processing.

For example:

~~~http
POST /api/products
~~~

The request body might contain the new product.

~~~json
{
  "name": "Running shoes",
  "price": 89.99
}
~~~

If the operation succeeds, the server will often respond with `201 Created`.

### PUT — replace a resource

`PUT` is generally used to replace an existing resource with a new representation.

For example:

~~~http
PUT /api/products/42
~~~

You might send the complete product representation:

~~~json
{
  "name": "Running shoes",
  "price": 99.99,
  "stock": 25
}
~~~

The important idea is that PUT commonly represents replacing the resource's representation.

### PATCH — partially update a resource

`PATCH` is useful when you only want to change part of a resource.

For example, if you only want to change the price:

~~~http
PATCH /api/products/42
~~~

The body could be:

~~~json
{
  "price": 99.99
}
~~~

You do not necessarily need to send every property of the product.

### DELETE — remove a resource

`DELETE` is used to request that a resource be removed.

For example:

~~~http
DELETE /api/products/42
~~~

The server might respond with `204 No Content` if the deletion succeeded and there is nothing else to return.

## An HTTP response

After receiving a request, the server sends a response.

~~~widget http-explorer
~~~

A response contains three important pieces:

- **Status code** — tells the client what happened.
- **Headers** — provide additional information.
- **Body** — contains returned data when there is data to return.

For example:

~~~http
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Content-Type: application/json
Location: /api/products/42

{
  "id": 42,
  "name": "Running shoes",
  "price": 89.99
}
~~~

The status code is `201`. The response body contains JSON describing the newly created product.

The `Location` header tells the client where the newly created resource can be found.

## Status code families

HTTP status codes have three digits. The first digit tells you the broad category.

~~~diagram
{"type": "layers", "title": "Status code families", "caption": "The first digit tells you who has to act: 2xx nobody, 3xx the browser, 4xx the client, 5xx the server team.", "layers": [{"label": "2xx Success", "items": ["200 OK", "201 Created", "204 No Content"], "highlight": true}, {"label": "3xx Redirect", "items": ["301 Moved Permanently", "304 Not Modified"]}, {"label": "4xx Client error", "items": ["400 Bad Request", "401 Unauthorized", "403 Forbidden", "404 Not Found", "409 Conflict"]}, {"label": "5xx Server error", "items": ["500 Internal Server Error", "503 Service Unavailable"]}]}
~~~

| Range | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 100–199 | Informational |
| 200–299 | Success |
| 300–399 | Redirect |
| 400–499 | Client error |
| 500–599 | Server error |

You do not need to memorize every HTTP status code. Start with the common ones.

## Successful responses

### 200 OK

`200 OK` means the request succeeded.

A GET request that successfully retrieves data will commonly return `200`.

### 201 Created

`201 Created` means the request successfully created something.

A successful POST that creates a new resource often returns `201`.

### 204 No Content

`204 No Content` means the request succeeded, but the server has no response body to return.

This is commonly useful after operations such as deleting a resource.

## Redirects and caching

### 301 and 302

`301 Moved Permanently` indicates that a resource has permanently moved to another location.

`302 Found` is commonly used for a temporary redirect.

Browsers can follow redirects automatically, so you may not always notice them directly.

### 304 Not Modified

`304 Not Modified` is closely related to caching. It tells the browser that a cached version of a resource can still be used because the resource has not changed according to the server's validation rules.

This can save bandwidth and make websites faster.

## Client errors

A **client error** generally means something about the request is wrong or the client is not allowed to perform the requested operation.

### 400 Bad Request

`400 Bad Request` usually means the server could not process the request because it was invalid.

For example, a JSON request might contain invalid data or an incorrectly formatted value.

### 401 Unauthorized

`401 Unauthorized` means the request lacks valid authentication credentials in a situation where authentication is required.

For example, an API might require a valid access token.

Despite the name, think of `401` primarily as an authentication problem.

### 403 Forbidden

`403 Forbidden` means the server understood the request but refuses to allow it.

For example, you might be logged in but not have permission to delete another user's account.

A useful distinction is:

~~~text
401 → Who are you?
403 → I know who you are, but you cannot do this.
~~~

### 404 Not Found

`404 Not Found` means the requested resource could not be found.

For example:

~~~http
GET /api/products/999999
~~~

might return `404` if that product does not exist.

### 409 Conflict

`409 Conflict` means the request conflicts with the current state of the resource.

For example, an API might reject an attempt to create a username that is already in use.

## Server errors

A **server error** means something went wrong while the server was trying to handle the request.

### 500 Internal Server Error

`500 Internal Server Error` is a general server-side failure.

As a developer, seeing a 500 response often means you should investigate the backend logs and the request that caused the problem.

### 503 Service Unavailable

`503 Service Unavailable` means the server is currently unable to handle the request.

This can happen when a service is temporarily overloaded, unavailable, or undergoing maintenance.

Do not automatically assume every 500 or 503 response means your frontend is broken. The problem may be entirely on the backend or infrastructure side.

## JSON is everywhere

**JSON** (JavaScript Object Notation) is a text format commonly used for exchanging structured data between frontend and backend applications.

For example:

~~~json
{
  "id": 42,
  "name": "Running shoes",
  "price": 89.99,
  "available": true
}
~~~

JSON is popular because it is relatively easy for humans to read and easy for programs to process.

A React frontend might send JSON to Spring Boot:

~~~text
React
  ↓ JSON
Spring Boot
  ↓
PostgreSQL
~~~

Spring Boot can process the request and return another JSON response.

You will work with this pattern extensively throughout the course.

## HTTP is stateless

HTTP is generally described as **stateless**, meaning each request is treated as its own request rather than automatically remembering previous requests. A server does not inherently know that two requests came from the same person just because they arrived one after another. Applications can add state using mechanisms such as cookies, sessions, and authentication tokens. A **cookie** is a small piece of data that a browser stores and sends back to a server on matching requests, which can help an application remember things such as a login session or preferences.

## Watching HTTP in your browser

You do not have to guess what a website is doing. Your browser can show you the actual network communication.

Open your browser's **Developer Tools** and find the **Network** tab. Then reload a page.

You will see requests for resources such as:

- HTML documents
- CSS files
- JavaScript files
- Images
- Fonts
- API requests

Click one of the requests and inspect its details.

Depending on your browser, you can usually find sections showing the request URL, method, status code, request headers, response headers, and response body.

This is one of the most useful debugging tools you will learn.

For example, if your React application displays an empty product list, the Network tab can help answer questions such as:

> Did the request happen?

> What URL was requested?

> Was it a GET or POST?

> Did the server return 200, 404, or 500?

> What data did the server actually return?

Learning to ask these questions will save you a lot of debugging time.

## Your first fetch()

JavaScript provides the **Fetch API** for making HTTP requests from the browser.

A simple GET request looks like this:

~~~js
fetch('/api/products')
  .then(response => response.json())
  .then(products => {
    console.log(products);
  });
~~~

`fetch()` starts an HTTP request and returns a **Promise**. A Promise represents the eventual result of an asynchronous operation.

The first `.then()` receives the HTTP response. Calling `response.json()` reads the response body and parses it as JSON.

You can also use `async` and `await`, which often makes application code easier to read:

~~~js
async function loadProducts() {
  const response = await fetch('/api/products');
  const products = await response.json();

  console.log(products);
}
~~~

There is an important detail here: `fetch()` does not automatically treat every HTTP error status as a rejected Promise. A response with status `404` or `500` can still produce a successful fetch operation, so application code often checks `response.ok` or `response.status` explicitly.

For example:

~~~js
const response = await fetch('/api/products');

if (!response.ok) {
  throw new Error(`Request failed: ${response.status}`);
}
~~~

This small detail becomes important when you start connecting React to Spring Boot.

## A complete HTTP conversation

Put everything together and a realistic API interaction might look like this:

~~~diagram
{"type": "sequence", "title": "Loading a task list", "actors": ["Browser", "API", "Database"], "steps": [{"from": "Browser", "to": "API", "label": "GET /api/tasks"}, {"from": "API", "to": "Database", "label": "SELECT * FROM task"}, {"from": "Database", "to": "API", "label": "3 rows", "dashed": true}, {"note": "rows → JSON", "over": "API"}, {"from": "API", "to": "Browser", "label": "200 OK + JSON array", "dashed": true}, {"from": "Browser", "to": "Browser", "label": "render list"}]}
~~~

~~~text
React
  ↓
POST /api/products
  ↓
Spring Boot
  ↓
validate data
  ↓
PostgreSQL
  ↓
Spring Boot
  ↓
201 Created + JSON
  ↓
React
  ↓
update the interface
~~~

The browser is therefore not simply "loading a page". Modern web applications are constantly making HTTP requests to exchange information.

## A short recap

When you work with HTTP, remember the basic conversation:

1. **The client sends a request.** It contains a method, URL, headers, and sometimes a body.
2. **The server processes the request.** A backend such as Spring Boot may validate data and communicate with PostgreSQL.
3. **The server sends a response.** It contains a status code, headers, and sometimes a body.
4. **The status code gives you the broad result.** `2xx` means success, `4xx` usually means a client-side request problem, and `5xx` indicates a server-side problem.
5. **JSON is a common format for API data.** React and Spring Boot can use it to exchange structured information.
6. **The Network tab lets you see what is really happening.** When something goes wrong, inspect the request instead of guessing.

Once you understand requests and responses, APIs become much less mysterious. They are structured conversations between programs, and HTTP provides many of the rules for that conversation.
takeaways: An HTTP request contains a method, URL, headers, and optionally a body.
GET reads, POST commonly creates, PUT replaces, PATCH partially updates, and DELETE removes resources.
Status codes use families: 2xx means success, 3xx redirects, 4xx client errors, and 5xx server errors.
JSON is a common format for sending structured data between React and Spring Boot.
The browser Network tab and fetch() are essential tools for understanding and debugging HTTP communication.

quiz.question: Which HTTP method is normally used to retrieve a resource?
quiz.explanation: GET is normally used to retrieve data without asking the server to create or modify the resource.

quiz.question: What does HTTP status code 201 usually mean?
options: The requested resource was not found.
quiz.explanation: 201 Created indicates that the request successfully resulted in the creation of a resource.

quiz.question: What does a 404 response usually indicate?
options: The requested resource was not found.
The server created a new resource.
quiz.explanation: 404 Not Found means the server could not find the requested resource.

quiz.question: Which status code family represents server errors?
quiz.explanation: HTTP status codes from 500 through 599 indicate server-side errors or unavailable server services.

quiz.question: Where can you inspect the HTTP requests made by a web page?
options: The browser's Network tab in Developer Tools.
quiz.explanation: The Network tab in browser Developer Tools shows requests, responses, status codes, headers, timing, and response data.

exercise.title: Classify HTTP status codes
exercise.task: Create two top-level functions named `describeStatus(code)` and `isRetryable(code)`. `describeStatus(code)` must return `"informational"`, `"success"`, `"redirect"`, `"client error"`, or `"server error"` according to the HTTP status code family, and it must return `"unknown"` for values outside 100–599 or for non-integers. `isRetryable(code)` must return `true` only for the status codes 408, 429, 500, 502, 503, and 504, and `false` for every other value. Do not rely on console output; the tests call these two functions directly.
exercise.hint: First validate that the value is an integer between 100 and 599. For the family, compare the code with 200, 300, 400, and 500; for retryable codes, an array with `includes()` is simple and readable.

tests.name: It classifies all status families
tests.code: return describeStatus(100) === 'informational' && describeStatus(200) === 'success' && describeStatus(300) === 'redirect' && describeStatus(400) === 'client error' && describeStatus(500) === 'server error';

tests.name: It handles boundary status codes
tests.code: return describeStatus(199) === 'informational' && describeStatus(299) === 'success' && describeStatus(399) === 'redirect' && describeStatus(499) === 'client error' && describeStatus(599) === 'server error';
